stages.name: Nationalisation
stages.title: Nationalisation
stages.sub: Understand what nationalisation means and weigh its main advantages and disadvantages against private ownership.

steps.q: A struggling private rail company is bought by the government and run by a state body instead of shareholders. Who now owns it?
steps.hint: Think about who receives the profits and controls decisions after the takeover.

steps.q: A private rail firm closes an unprofitable rural line to protect profit. A state-owned rail firm could choose to keep it open even if it loses money. Why might it do this?
steps.right: To protect jobs and serve passengers, not just make profit
steps.wrong: Because it still needs to maximise shareholder returns
steps.hint: The state firm does not answer to shareholders chasing profit in the same way.
steps.pre: So state ownership lets government put people and services ahead of profit, an

steps.q: A steel plant's pollution harms nearby residents, but a private owner ignores this cost because it doesn't hit their profits. If the government owned the plant instead, could it now force the true social cost to be taken into account?
steps.right: Yes, it can build that cost into its decisions
steps.wrong: No, ownership doesn't change whose costs count
steps.hint: Who decides what counts in the firm's decisions once government is the owner?
steps.pre: So the effect on others outside the transaction can now be considered, an

steps.q: Electricity supply is vital even in a crisis when a private firm might go bankrupt and stop investing. Would a government want to guarantee this service keeps running regardless of profitability?
steps.right: Yes, because it's too important to risk losing
steps.wrong: No, profitability should always come first for such services
steps.hint: Think about services the whole country depends on, not just about revenue.
steps.pre: So nationalisation can build in outside costs/benefits and guarantee key services, an

steps.q: A private firm's managers know that poor performance risks their jobs and bonuses, since profit is closely watched by owners. If a state manager knows the firm will be funded regardless of performance, are they under the same pressure to cut costs and work efficiently?
steps.right: No, the pressure to be efficient is weaker
steps.wrong: Yes, the pressure is exactly the same
steps.hint: Without profit and owners watching closely, what happens to the incentive to be lean and effective?
steps.pre: So removing the profit motive can weaken the drive for efficiency, a

steps.q: Compare a firm before and after nationalisation: before, profit went to private shareholders; after, any surplus (or loss) belongs to the state and decisions may prioritise service over returns. What happens to the profit actually earned or targeted by the firm?
steps.right: It tends to fall, since profit is no longer the main goal
steps.wrong: It stays exactly the same as under private ownership
steps.hint: Think about what the firm is now aiming for instead of maximising returns.
